USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue the Osaka truce and pursue the resumed negotiations with China, holding existing tariffs in place as leverage without imposing new tariffs and without unilateral concessions. Do not escalate (that would break the truce and compound the yield-curve stress already visible), but also do not give ground on Huawei removal or the enforcement mechanism until Beijing makes firm, verifiable commitments on agricultural purchases and structural reform. Maintain the current posture while the working-level talks (Lighthizer/Mnuchin-Liu contact) gather momentum.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to U.S. interests is real but bounded — positive but moderate (+0.3). The bond market is signaling genuine economic strain from the trade war: the 10-yr Treasury yield collapsed from ~2.74% to ~2.06% and the 2-yr from ~2.58% to ~1.83% over the window (country_health DGS10/DGS2), a flattening curve indicating growth concern and expected Fed easing, while industrial production ticked down (INDPRO to ~101.9) — a material, if not existential, drag on sentiment and capex. However, this is not existential: consumer sentiment is robust (UMCSENT ~98.4), inflation is contained (CPI ~255.8), and the immediate escalation threat was defused at Osaka, where Washington suspended new tariffs on the ~$300B basket and agreed to resume talks while keeping existing tariffs (event_timeline 2019-06-29; Reuters/NPR/BBC, 2019-06-29/07-02). Because the truce has removed the near-term escalation cliff and the U.S. retains the leverage of ~$250B in 25% tariffs plus Huawei on the Entity List, the contentious state is a manageable standoff rather than a crisis. On the action axis, escalation would be counterproductive — markets already fear the trade war's drag and breaking the truce would risk the recession signal the yield curve is flashing; unilateral concession is also premature since Beijing has not made firm purchase commitments and still demands removal of all tariffs (Bloomberg 2019-07-05, Globe and Mail 2019-07-10). Hence hold/negotiate at 0.0 is the disciplined stance: keep the pressure credible, extract verifiable concessions, and wait — with Huawei's Temporary General License running to Aug 19 and licensing promised 'where there is no threat to national security' (HK Law/RCR Wireless, 2019-07-10/16), the U.S. can calibrate relief to progress rather than concede in advance.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold our posture and continue the resumed talks without committing to new purchases or structural concessions, while quietly preserving our leverage (rare earths, unreliable entity list). Do not escalate — a fresh tariff or retaliation move would collapse the fragile Osaka truce and compound domestic slowdown. Press, in return, for concrete and verifiable US relief (most importantly actual easing—not just promise—of the Huawei entity-list restrictions and staying below the threatened ~$300B additional tariff tranche).

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is real but bounded, not existential. The US has List 3 at 25% on ~$250B of our exports (May 10) and has placed Huawei plus 68 affiliates on the Entity List restricting US components (May 16), directly threatening a flagship sector — consistent with the high (+0.5) firm-level anchor. Yet crushing near-term escalation has paused: at Osaka (June 29) both sides agreed to resume talks with no new tariffs 'for the time being,' though existing tariffs remain. Mitigating factors keep this from existential: China's FX reserves rose $18.23B to $3.119T in June, the yuan gained 0.6% (first monthly rise since Feb), bearish yuan bets halved, and offshore investors bought Chinese sovereign debt at a record pace on the truce — no financial-stability stress. The domestic cost is concentrated in a slowing economy (factory activity contracting, Q2 GDP set to slow further, PBOC RRR cuts expected), which argues against aggressive escalation that would deepen the slowdown. Critically, US pain is visible (10y yield fell ~2.74% to ~2.06%, Baa spreads tightened, US IP declining, Fed easing expected), supplying genuine bargaining leverage. On that basis I set threat at +0.4 (materially high, not existential) and action at +0.1 — engage, do not escalate, and extract reciprocal US concessions before any purchase commitments, which is premature while Huawei relief has not actually been delivered (a July 16 legal analysis confirms no BIS action removing Huawei yet).
